section_summary: This section documents official investigations, inter-agency communications, and field reports assessing Japan's critical postwar food deficit between early 1945 and spring 1946. Comprehensive reports compiled by the Foreign Economic Administration and SCAP's Natural Resources Section detail declining agricultural yields, farmer quota resistance, and the urgent necessity of emergency food imports to prevent mass urban starvation. Communications between SCAP, the State Department, the War Department, and the Department of Agriculture reflect mounting concern over food allocations amidst a worldwide grain shortage.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting an inquiry from the Department of Agriculture on agricultural and food conditions in Japan and occupied areas.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet citing a despatch from Vladivostok regarding the Department of Agriculture's request for agricultural and food data.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Request of Department of Agriculture for Current Information on Agricultural Production

subfiles.about: Consular despatch reporting on the scarcity of commercial and official intelligence in Calcutta regarding food conditions in Japan and occupied territories.
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Calcutta
subfiles.summary: The Consul General reports that primary food data is unavailable in Calcutta and suggests consulting FEA and military sources in Washington.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 867: Request from Department of Agriculture for Current Information on Agricultural Production

subfiles.about: Department of State inquiry to SCAP regarding reported relaxations of Japanese food rationing and crop collection controls.
subfiles.summary: The State Department asks whether reported relaxations in food rationing and vegetable price controls are genuine and required by domestic conditions.
subfiles.title: Telegram to SCAP Tokyo on Food Rationing Regulations and Controls
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo (George Atcheson, Jr. / Charles A. Willoughby)

subfiles.about: Department of State cable questioning whether Japanese food import requests above 1,500-1,700 calories can be justified.
subfiles.summary: State doubts providing more than 1,500 to 1,700 calories daily given worldwide shortages and Far Eastern Advisory Commission policy.
subfiles.title: Telegram to SCAP Tokyo regarding Japanese Food Requirements
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo (George Atcheson, Jr.)

subfiles.about: Comprehensive study by the Foreign Economic Administration analyzing Japanese food production, consumption, and deficits during 1941-1945.
subfiles.from: Foreign Economic Administration, Enemy Branch, Food and Agriculture Division
subfiles.summary: This detailed monograph examines the deterioration of Japan's domestic food position from 1941 through 1945. It provides commodity breakdowns for rice, grains, pulses, and marine products, noting that carry-over stocks were exhausted by late 1943. Average per capita daily consumption dropped to approximately 1,809 calories in 1945, with urban populations facing acute vulnerability. Statistical tables and War Department intelligence outline projected shortages and necessary import priorities for 1946.
subfiles.title: Wartime Food Position of Japan Proper with Special Reference to 1945

subfiles.about: SCAP response clarifying that food rationing controls have not been relaxed and outlining measures to enforce farm collections.
subfiles.from: George Atcheson, Jr., Acting Political Adviser, SCAP
subfiles.summary: SCAP confirms staple rationing continues unchanged, explaining that farm price increases and perishable ceiling adjustments were adopted to combat black markets.
subfiles.title: Incoming Telegram No. 209 (CA 56110) on Maintenance of Rationing Controls

subfiles.about: Letter transmitting a proposed radiogram to SCAP concerning the impact of the global food crisis on Japanese import prospects.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Martin submits a draft message to SCAP emphasizing global food deficits and suggesting cotton textile distribution to incentivize farmers to deliver crops.
subfiles.title: Letter to Lt. Col. Ernest Gross Enclosing Draft Radiogram 'Japanese Food Imports'
subfiles.to: Lt. Colonel Ernest Gross, Civil Affairs Division, War Department

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting SCAP Natural Resources Section Report No. 10 analyzing Japan's anticipated food position and import needs for 1946.
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo (John S. Service)
subfiles.summary: This despatch transmits Natural Resources Section Report No. 10, 'Food Position of Japan Proper in 1946', dated December 27, 1945. The report details poor harvest yields caused by typhoons and floods, projecting an indigenous food availability of only 1,325 calories per person per day. It highlights urban-rural distribution disparities, farmer quota withholding, and inflation. Detailed statistical appendices evaluate food import requirements under various calorie targets and summarize Japanese official import requests.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 185 Transmitting Report on Food Position of Japan Proper in 1946 (NRS Report No. 10)

subfiles.about: Letter from a former FEA intelligence officer reporting on food conditions in Japan and requesting permission to publish his findings.
subfiles.summary: Mackenzie reports his field observations in Japan to State Department officials and asks permission to publish a rewritten version in a magazine.
subfiles.title: Letter from Albert Haynes Mackenzie Regarding Field Report on Japanese Food Problem
subfiles.to: George Carter Vincent, Chief, Far East Division, Department of State

subfiles.about: State Department letter authorizing Albert H. Mackenzie to publish a revised version of his Japanese food report.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Chief, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.summary: The State Department grants permission to publish the food report provided it contains no indication of official State Department origin.
subfiles.title: Letter to Albert H. Mackenzie Granting Permission to Publish Food Report

subfiles.about: Letter transmitting a draft radiogram to SCAP questioning preliminary findings of an urban nutritional survey in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Martin forwards a draft radiogram asking SCAP to explain how reported Tokyo intakes of 1,971 calories reconcile with asserted import emergencies.
subfiles.title: Letter to Lt. Col. Ernest Gross Enclosing Draft Radiogram on Tokyo Nutritional Survey
subfiles.to: Lt. Colonel Ernest Gross, Civil Affairs Division, War Department

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum concerning General MacArthur's urgent cable warning of impending starvation in Japan and an emergency White House meeting.
subfiles.from: Civil Affairs Division, War Department (Colonel Gay via staff)
subfiles.summary: Colonel Gay informs Claxton that MacArthur anticipates urban starvation after May 1, prompting an urgent inter-agency White House conference.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for Mr. Claxton Regarding General MacArthur's Urgent Food Cable

subfiles.about: State Department communication assessing Japanese food requirements and recommending an emergency March grain shipment.
subfiles.from: Donald D. Kennedy, Chief, International Resources Division
subfiles.summary: Kennedy concurs that urban supplies face spring exhaustion and recommends scheduling an initial emergency shipment to Japan in March.
subfiles.title: Letter to D. A. FitzGerald on Japanese Food Requirements and Spring Allocations
subfiles.to: D. A. FitzGerald, Director, Office of Requirements and Allocations, Department of Agriculture

subfiles.about: Commercial inquiry from an American company regarding procedures for importing agar-agar from Japan.
subfiles.from: S. A. Marshak, The Energy Food Co.
subfiles.summary: The Energy Food Co. requests guidance on which government department handles purchasing Japanese agar-agar.
subfiles.title: Inquiry from The Energy Food Co. Concerning Japanese Agar-Agar

subfiles.about: State Department reply explaining that commercial imports of Japanese products are handled by the U.S. Commercial Company.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Martin informs Marshak that Japanese agar-agar will be exported in limited quantities through the U.S. Commercial Company in Washington.
subfiles.title: Letter to S. A. Marshak Regarding Purchase of Japanese Agar-Agar
subfiles.to: S. A. Marshak, The Energy Food Company

subfiles.about: Field telegram reporting results of a civilian feeding investigation in Japan and urgently requesting monthly cereal shipments.
subfiles.summary: Harrison confirms civilian feeding requirements are realistic and urges high-priority shipments of 200,000 tons of grain monthly for March through May.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Harrison to Secretary Anderson and Assistant Secretary Clayton
subfiles.to: Clinton P. Anderson, Secretary of Agriculture, and William L. Clayton, Assistant Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Correction telegram rectifying a typographical error in Harrison's cable of March 16.
subfiles.summary: Corrects page two, line twenty-four of Harrison's telegram to read 'non-self suppliers' instead of 'non-self injurious'.
subfiles.title: Correction Telegram from Harrison to Secretary Anderson and Assistant Secretary Clayton
subfiles.to: Clinton P. Anderson, Secretary of Agriculture, and William L. Clayton, Assistant Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting a memorandum by Charles J. Shohan and warning of grave political consequences if famine strikes Japan.
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Foreign Service Officer, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Bishop transmits Charles J. Shohan's memorandum warning of an imminent May-July food crisis. Bishop emphasizes that widespread famine would cause severe civil disorder, undermine occupation objectives, and drive the Japanese populace toward communism. Shohan's memorandum details declining urban rations, farmer withholding, and the depletion of controlled grain reserves.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 337: Food Crisis in Japan (Enclosing Memorandum by Charles J. Shohan)

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing Soviet press coverage of Allied discussions on Japanese food shipments, voting irregularities, and Tokyo Bay treasure.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Tass items including New Zealand's Far Eastern Commission objection to proposed U.S. deliveries of 500,000 tons of food to Japan.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 110 from Moscow Reporting Soviet Press Coverage on Japan
